To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the National Emphysemma Treatment Trial was a multicenter, randomized controlled trial comparing lung-volume-reduction-surgery (LVRS) with medical treatment for patients with severe emphysemma.

the subgroup of patients at risk for harm was identified by the Data and Safety and Monitoring Board and that the National Heart, Blood, and Lung Institute, the sponsor of the trial, accepted this recommendation.
the National EmphyseMA Treatment Trial was a multicenter clinical trial of patients with severe emphyseMA that was stopped early because of a subgroup analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the methodologic aspects of terminating enrollment of a sub-group of patients in a randomized controlled trial.
the methodologic issues in terminating the enrollment of a subgroup in a multicenter clinical trial.
the operational aspects of terminating enrollment of a subset of patients in a clinical trial.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the subgroup of patients with upper lobe emphysema and carbon monoxide diffusing capacity (D LCO) less than 20% of the predicted value are at significantly higher risk for 30-day mortality without counterbalancing improvement in exercise capacity.
LVRS is an effective therapy for patients with severe emphysematous destruction of the upper lobes, but not in those with severe destruction of the lower lobes.
the trial was terminated for safety reasons in a subgroup of patients, but that the trial continues for efficacy in other subgroups.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the trial's sponsor and the Data and Safety and Monitoring Board acted in the best interest of the patients, the trial and the research community.

the NETT investigators, the Data and Monitoring Board, the Research Group and the National Heart, Blood, and Lung Institute were successful in implementing the recommendation to terminate further randomization in a subgroup of patients at increased risk.

the National EmphyseMA Treatment Trial was successful in defining subgroups of patients with differential outcomes, in identifying patients at risk of adverse events from LVRS, and in terminating enrollment of such patients in a timely manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decision to terminate the enrollment of a subgroup is a complex process that requires the cooperation and understanding of all parties involved, as well as the support of the medical community.

it is possible to implement a change in the protocol for a large multicenter trial in a timely and effective way, but it is important to anticipate and plan for the potential negative impact of such an action on the trial's participants and the medical community.

, when a subgroup of patients is identified as being at high risk of harm from a treatment, the decision of whether to terminate randomization of such a subgroup is a complex one, and should be made by the sponsor of the study in collaboration with the Data and Safety and Monitoring Board, the trial's investigators, the institutional committees and the patients.
